slide.title: Direct the Camera
slide.body: Centre: simple camera icon. Around it, four teal arrows labelled pan, tilt, dolly, orbit. Small tag: AI Video Production and Motion · Lesson 4.

scenes.voiceover: Ask a video model for a woman in a café, and you get a random camera, random light and random movement. Ask for a slow dolly-in on a woman reading in warm window light, and the result looks planned.

slide.title: Speaking the Language of the Camera
slide.body: AI Video Production and Motion · Lesson 4 of 14

scenes.voiceover: The difference is the language of the camera. In the last lesson, you built a shot list. Now you learn the words that turn each row into a clear prompt.

slide.title: Image prompt + two new parts
slide.body: Four grey boxes: subject · setting · lighting · style. Plus sign. Two teal boxes: movement · time.

scenes.voiceover: First, a quick recap from AI Image Generation. A good image prompt names the subject, the setting, the lighting and the style, and it is specific. All of that still applies. Video adds two things: movement and time.

slide.title: Three shot types
slide.body: Three frames of the same café scene side by side. Wide: whole café, shows where we are. Medium: person from the waist up, shows what they do. Close-up: hands on a cup, shows detail and emotion.

scenes.voiceover: Shot types describe how much the viewer sees. A wide shot shows the whole scene, so we know where we are. A medium shot shows a person from about the waist up, so we see what they are doing. A close-up shows a face, hands or a small object. It shows detail and emotion.

slide.title: Camera movements, part 1
slide.body: Camera icon with animated arrows, revealed one by one: Pan (turns left or right) · Tilt (turns up or down) · Dolly in / out (moves towards or away).

scenes.voiceover: Camera movements describe how the view changes. A pan turns the camera left or right from one spot. A tilt turns it up or down. A dolly moves the camera towards the subject, or away from it.

scenes.stock_query: camera moving in circle around person
scenes.voiceover: An orbit moves the camera in a circle around the subject. Handheld adds small, natural shaking, as if a person holds the camera. And static means the camera does not move at all.

slide.title: Pacing words
slide.body: slow · gentle · steady · fast · time-lapse · slow motion. Highlighted rule at the bottom: One movement per shot.

scenes.voiceover: Pacing words tell the model about speed. Slow, gentle, steady, fast, time-lapse, slow motion. Here is an important rule. Use one movement per shot. Two or three movements in a short clip often produce confused results.

slide.title: The seven-part formula
slide.body: Header: Subject + Action + Setting + Camera movement + Lighting + Style + Duration. Below, the fisherman prompt from content.md word for word, each part in a different colour with its label: 'A young fisherman in a yellow raincoat (subject) pulls a net onto a small wooden boat (action) on a grey sea near a rocky coast (setting). Slow dolly-in from a medium shot to a close-up of his hands (camera movement). Soft overcast morning light (lighting). Realistic documentary style, natural colours (style). 6 seconds (duration).'

scenes.voiceover: Now put it together. The video prompt formula in this course has seven parts. Subject, action, setting, camera movement, lighting, style and duration. On screen, you can see an example: a young fisherman pulls a net onto a small boat, with a slow dolly-in to his hands, in soft overcast light.

slide.title: A checklist, not a guarantee
slide.body: Duration: in the prompt or in a menu, keep it in your notes · Models respond differently to the same words · Use the formula as a checklist

scenes.voiceover: Some tools set the duration in a menu, not in the prompt. Keep it in your notes anyway, so your plan and your settings match. And different models respond differently to the same words. So treat the formula as a checklist, not a guarantee.

scenes.stock_query: film director talking to camera operator on set
scenes.voiceover: Think of a prompt as the notes a director gives a camera operator before a take. Start wide, move in slowly, keep the light soft. A good operator follows short, clear notes. Long, mixed-up notes produce a confused take.

scenes.stock_query: bright minimal bathroom with plant morning light
scenes.voiceover: Let's see an example. Hana runs a small skincare brand in Busan, South Korea. Her shot list row says: close-up, hand applies cream, bathroom, morning.

slide.title: From row to prompt
slide.body: Top, small: shot list row 'Close-up | Hand applies cream | Bathroom, morning'. Below, Hana's prompt from content.md word for word: 'A woman's hand with short natural nails gently spreads white cream on the back of her other hand. A bright, minimal bathroom with a white sink and a green plant. Static close-up, very slight slow push-in. Soft morning daylight from a window on the left. Clean, modern commercial style, pastel colours. 5 seconds.'

scenes.voiceover: She turns that short row into a full prompt. You can see it on screen. A woman's hand gently spreads white cream on her other hand, in a bright, minimal bathroom. A static close-up with a very slight push-in, soft morning light from the left, a clean commercial style, and five seconds.

scenes.broll_prompt: A woman's hand with short natural nails gently spreads white cream on the back of her other hand, in a bright minimal bathroom with a white sink and a green plant; static close-up with a very slight slow push-in; soft morning daylight from a window on the left; clean modern commercial style, pastel colours; 5 seconds; hands only, no face, no readable text, no labels, no logos.
scenes.voiceover: This is the kind of clip a prompt like that can produce. Nothing surprising happens. The camera does exactly what Hana asked for.

slide.title: Formula check
slide.body: Subject: a woman's hand ✓ · Action: spreads cream ✓ · Setting: bright bathroom ✓ · Camera: static close-up, slight push-in ✓ · Lighting: morning daylight from the left ✓ · Style: clean commercial ✓ · Duration: 5 seconds ✓

scenes.voiceover: Then she checks it against the formula. The subject is a woman's hand. The action is spreading cream. The setting is a bright bathroom. The camera is a static close-up with a slight push-in. Then the lighting, the style and the duration. All seven parts are there.

slide.title: Three movements, or one?
slide.body: Left, crossed out: 'camera orbits around her while zooming in and panning to the window' (three movements). Right, ticked: 'Static close-up, very slight slow push-in' (one movement).

scenes.voiceover: Her first draft was different. It said the camera orbits around her while zooming in and panning to the window. That is three movements in five seconds. They usually look unnatural, so she removed them.

A common mistake is to describe the scene carefully and forget the camera. The model then chooses a movement for you, often a slow drift that does not match the next shot. So always choose one clear movement, or static.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Shot types: how much we see. Movements: how the view changes. 2. Subject + Action + Setting + Camera + Lighting + Style + Duration. 3. One movement per shot; the formula is a checklist.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, shot types control how much the viewer sees, and camera movements control how the view changes. Second, the formula is subject, action, setting, camera movement, lighting, style and duration. Third, use one movement per short shot, and treat the formula as a checklist.

scenes.on_screen_text: Next: Keyframes, From Still Image to Motion
scenes.voiceover: Now it is your turn. Choose four rows from your shot list, including a close-up and a wide shot, and rewrite them as full prompts with all seven parts. Check each one has exactly one movement. It takes about twenty-five minutes. Next lesson: Keyframes, From Still Image to Motion. See you there.
